$comment: Design language, not cars. Every entry describes an era, a set of constraints that produced a
shape, and real proportions in metres — the things that actually steer a generator — plus an
`avoid` list naming what must not appear. Nothing here names a marque, a model or a team: a
prompt that names one gets a copy of that one, which is the outcome this file exists to prevent.
See README.md for why each field is shaped the way it is.
FIELDS. `subject` is the noun the prompt uses, so it must read as a thing and not as a slot name.
`kind` is the ModelDef kind in apps/coast/src/render/models.ts that this replaces, or null with
`newKind: true` for an asset the game has no slot for yet — generating one of those is fine, but
promoting it means adding a ModelDef and putting it in a scene's roadside or landmark list.
`dims` is read by proportion.mjs as well as by the prompt: lengthM/spanM run left-to-right,
widthM and depthM across, and the optional wheelDiameterM, poleHeightM and legHeightM are what
turn a plain envelope box into a drawing with the right mass in the right place.
KEEP CUES SHORT. generate.mjs budgets the prompt at 1800 characters and gives way at the END of
the cue list when it runs over, loudly. Six or seven cues is the working size; a spec with twelve
is not a richer spec, it is a spec whose last five lines were never read.

backgrounds.green: flat chroma-green #2ecc40, evenly lit, no gradient, no shadow cast on it, no ground under the object
backgrounds.magenta: saturated chroma-magenta #ff00ff, evenly lit, no gradient, no shadow cast on it, no ground under the object

$chroma: Green for everything except vegetation, and magenta for that. A leaf on a green screen is the
one case where the backdrop and the subject are the same colour: the first palm generation came
back with BROWN fronds, because the prompt has to say the object is never the key colour and the
model obeyed. Magenta costs nothing and asks nothing of the plant. Per-spec `chroma` overrides
the class default — put a red car on green, never on magenta.
defaults.camera: camera level with the subject's mid-height, no perspective distortion, the whole object in frame with a small margin
defaults.style: a clean simple 3D model, flat bright arcade look: bold simple shapes, BRIGHT SATURATED colour, smooth clean surfaces, no photographic texture or grain, nothing under it
defaults.render: flat even lighting, no cast shadow, no ground, no base, no plinth, no soil, no rock under it — the object simply ends where it ends; no dirt, dust, rust, stains or weathering, nothing photographic
avoid: manufacturer badges, marque emblems, grille crests or wordmarks of any kind
real sponsor marks, oil-company colours, cigarette-brand liveries
model names or type numbers anywhere on the body
licence plates bearing real jurisdictions
watermarks, signatures, captions, UI, borders

styleByClass.architecture: Windows are flat dark panels, never reflective glass; walls are plain blocks of one colour; no reflections, no interior visible
styleByClass.signage: Flat painted panels in plain blocks of colour, no reflections
styleByClass.props: Plain painted metal in flat colour, no reflections

bible.says: IMAGE {n} is the PALETTE AND FINISH CHART. Match its colours, its surface finish and its soft flat shading exactly. It contains no objects: draw NOTHING from it, take only the look
bible.prompt:
A materials and palette chart for a late-1980s arcade racing game — NO objects, NO vehicles, NO scenery, NO buildings, nothing recognisable. Only plain geometric primitives on a plain neutral field: a sphere, a cube, a cylinder, a cone and a flat panel, repeated in a grid, each rendered in one bright saturated colour — red, orange, yellow, grass green, turquoise, royal blue, cream white.

The RENDERING is the point: smooth clean surfaces, flat even light, soft simple shading that shows the form, hard clean edges, no texture, no grain, no reflections, no shadows on the field, no gloss highlights blown out. Beneath them a row of flat colour swatches in the same palette.

No text, no lettering, no numbers, no labels.
bible.composedSays: In the REFERENCE: its right half is this object's measured side outline — match that silhouette, {dims}. Its left half is the palette and finish. Draw neither of them, draw the object

$engines: Two servers with opposite strengths, both measured rather than assumed.
DEV reads what you attach — so literally that a two-panel outline came back as a two-panel
drawing. That is the failure mode everywhere except where a shape must be obeyed, and for a
vehicle it must: asked for a mid-engined prototype against a plain box, every server returns a
long-nosed front-engined sports racer. Give dev a DRAWN PROFILE and it traces it. Dev discards
`reference_image` silently, so there is no style guide on this side; the words carry it.
KLEIN ignores attachments entirely — two completely different outlines under `image` produced
BYTE-IDENTICAL output — and reads `reference_image`, which refers rather than copies. So klein
is where the style guide works, and where proportion is only as good as the sentence describing
it. Right for scenery, whose shapes are generic and whose look is everything.
Hence `engineByClass`. A spec can override with its own `engine`.
